newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Banco do Brasil turned corner in '96.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Banco do Brasil turned corner in '96.

text.p: Brazilian federal bank Banco do Brasil posted a record loss in 1996, but bank officials said a return to the black in the second half of the year marked a new period of profitability ahead.

The bank said it went 7.52 billion reais into the red in 1996 after making a 254.9 million real profit in the second half, cutting slightly into the bank's massive first half loss of 7.8 billion reais.

"We have entered a new phase," said Banco do Brasil President Paulo Cesar Ximenes. "The profit in the second half is not everything we would wish, we expect more than that, but it is the start of a new period of profit."
In 1995, Banco do Brasil lost 4.2 billion reais, up to then the worst financial performance in its history.

Last March, it revealed it had to write off 5.5 billion reais in bad loans after reducing the period for which it considers debts to be overdue to 60 days from one year. It also lost over 1.0 billion reais in currency conversions dating back to 1994.
The gaping hole in the bank's accounts forced the government to inject 8.0 billion reais into its capital to prevent it from going under and officials pledged to end decades of political misuse.
Financial director Carlos Gilberto Caetano said total revenue from banking services last year was 13.2 billion reais.
He said since a restructuring plan was begun at the end of June, revenue from fees had risen 43 percent over 1995 levels and payroll costs had dropped 1.5 percent over the first half.
Caetano added that the level of bad loans had been cut back to 17.1 percent of the total from 26.2 percent.
"We are tackling our problems," he said.

Caetano said the bank's second half profit was equivalent to an annualized return on shareholders' equity of 9.3 percent, which he described as "not excellent, but not a bad result". Ximenes said his target was for a return of 12 percent.
In a statement, Banco do Brasil said the reduction in its non-performing loans portfolio was one of the main reasons for the reversal in the bank's fortunes after June.
The bank invested $200 million in technology in 1996 and will invest another $600 million in 1997 in order to improve customer services and attract new accounts.
Describing 1996 as a "year of great changes", the bank said it had turned the corner and become a more flexible, lean, efficient and profit-conscious organization.
It had shed 9,308 full-time and 7,033 part-time jobs and closed 76 loss-making branches.

Ximenes said the bank's fund management arm -- the largest in the country with some 18.3 billion reais distributed through 50 funds -- was the most profitable of the big fund adminstrators and would continue to perform well in 1997.
He said the bank was expanding its insurance operations, establishing joint ventures to sell life, health and vehicle insurance.
Banco do Brasil has frequently been used by governments in the past to provide soft loans for politically sensitive sectors, in particular agriculture.
Ximenes said the bank would continue to be the main source of funds for farmers.
"We will continue to be a public institution aimed mainly at financing agriculture. But we will also be more attuned to profit," he said.
((-- Brasilia newsroom 55-61-2230358))
